intake.question: Should we use an AI marketing tool to text all our past customers a fall tune-up promo?
intake.leaning: Yes, blast the whole list next week

must_catch.label: TCPA / prior express written consent for marketing texts

baseline:
# Recommendation

**Yes to the fall tune-up campaign, but not as a one-shot blast to the whole list next week.** Run it as a staged, consent-checked campaign, and use Housecall Pro's built-in marketing tools before paying for a new AI tool.

## Why

- Past customers are your cheapest source of fall bookings. They already know you, and tune-ups are a natural, expected offer.
- A new AI tool probably adds little. The AI part (writing copy, subject lines, variations) can be done in ChatGPT or similar for free or about $20/month. Housecall Pro already has customer lists, text/email campaigns, and can sell maintenance plans. Check what it includes before spending your $150.
- A blast is the riskiest way to do this: legal exposure, a flood of calls you can't handle, and angry customers.

## Main risks

1. **Texting consent and legal exposure.** Marketing texts to people who never agreed to receive them can violate the federal TCPA, which allows $500–$1,500 per message in lawsuits. Maryland also has its own telemarketing/robocall law. A customer who gave you their number for a service appointment is not automatically consenting to promotional texts. Check with an attorney or your tool's compliance guidance, since I can't give you a definitive legal read on your list.
2. **Carrier registration (10DLC).** Business texting in the U.S. requires registering your brand and campaign, which can take days to weeks. Unregistered blasts get filtered or blocked, and your number can get flagged. "Next week" may not be realistic with a new tool.
3. **Opt-out requirements.** Every message needs your business name and a clear "Reply STOP to opt out," and you must honor opt-outs immediately.
4. **Overwhelming 4 technicians.** If 15% of the list responds at once, you get a booking spike, phone chaos, and slow replies, which hurts reviews.
5. **List quality.** Old numbers, landlords, customers who moved, people you've had complaints with, and commercial accounts need different handling or exclusion.
6. **Discounting too deeply.** A big discount on tune-ups can train customers to wait for deals and eat margin.

## Next steps

**This week**
- Clean the list in Housecall Pro: remove bad numbers, past disputes, and anyone who opted out. Split into segments: customers from the last 12–24 months, older customers, and existing maintenance-plan members.
- Identify who has actually opted in to texts. Anyone without clear consent gets an email or postcard instead, or gets a text only after you've confirmed with legal guidance.
- Check Housecall Pro's marketing features and its text registration process. Ask support what it handles for compliance.

**Next 1–2 weeks**
- Write the offer. For example: "Fall furnace tune-up, $89 (normally $129), book by Oct 31," or a tune-up bundled with a maintenance plan sign-up. Maintenance plans are the real prize because they create recurring revenue and fill future slow seasons.
- Use AI to draft 2–3 message variations. Keep them short and personal, include your company name, a booking link or phone number, and opt-out language.
- Send a test to yourself and your team.

**Launch in waves**
- Wave 1: your most recent and most loyal customers, about 20–25% of the list. Watch response and booking volume for 2–3 days.
- Waves 2 and 3: send to the rest, spaced a week apart, adjusting to your open schedule.
- Send a single reminder to non-responders about 7–10 days later, not repeated texts.
- Send during business hours, avoid weekends and early mornings, and cap marketing texts at about 1–2 per month.

**Track**
- Messages sent, opt-out rate (above 2–3% means your message or list is off), bookings, revenue, and maintenance plan sign-ups.
- Compare cost and results against email and a simple postcard to older customers.

## Budget

Stay well under $150/month. The extra could go to a small Google Business Profile push or review requests after each tune-up, which help fill the schedule beyond this one campaign.

**Bottom line:** the campaign is a good idea. Sending to everyone at once, without checking consent and registration, is the part to avoid.

intake.question: Should we use an AI marketing tool to text all our past customers a fall tune-up promo?
intake.leaning: Yes, blast the whole list next week

evidence.decision: Whether to use an AI marketing tool to send a fall tune-up promotional text to the entire past-customer list of a 4-technician HVAC company in Frederick, Maryland, as early as next week.
options: Do nothing: keep the current fall schedule process (word of mouth, inbound calls, existing Housecall Pro reminders) and spend no new money.
Blast the whole past-customer list by text next week with an AI marketing or SMS tool, as the owner is leaning toward.
Send texts only to customers with documented written marketing-text consent. Reach everyone else by email, postcard or live phone calls, and start collecting written opt-ins on every job.

Add a standalone SMS platform with built-in opt-in and opt-out handling and 10DLC registration, then run a staged send. Start with consented contacts and expand as consent is gathered, after a lawyer reviews the consent language.

facts.claim: Maryland's Stop the Spam Calls Act (in effect Jan 1, 2024) requires prior express written consent for marketing texts sent through an 'automated system' for selecting or dialing numbers. It bars solicitations from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. and caps contacts at three in 24 hours on the same subject. Federal quiet hours are looser, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., so the state rule is stricter. Calls to Maryland area codes are presumed to reach Maryland residents.

A 2024 amendment (HB 1228, effective April 25, 2024) added a private right of action under the Maryland law: the greater of $500 or actual damages per violation, up to triple for willful or knowing violations. This is on top of an older Maryland statute that lets consumers sue for federal TCPA violations for $500 or actual damages plus attorney fees.

The Maryland exemptions are narrow. One compliance guide says there is no general exemption for texting past customers, and that Maryland's existing-business-relationship exemption covers only a contact that began as informational and became a sales pitch at the customer's request. Law-firm summaries of the Act do list an exemption for solicitations for maintenance or repair contracts on goods previously purchased from the solicitor. Whether it covers tune-ups on equipment this company installed is a legal question.

Federal TCPA statutory damages are $500 per violation, trebled to $1,500 if willful or knowing, so exposure scales with the number of texts sent. On Sept 30, 2026 the FCC adopted new opt-out rules. Senders may designate an exclusive opt-out method if they disclose it in each text. The standardized reply words (stop, quit, end, revoke, opt out, cancel, unsubscribe) must be honored. An opt-out from a marketing text still revokes consent for all future marketing texts.

Business texting from a standard 10-digit number requires carrier 10DLC registration. Typical costs are about $4 to $46 one-time for brand registration and vetting, about $15 per campaign, about $10 per month per campaign, and carrier surcharges of roughly $0.003 to $0.005 per text segment. Brand registration takes about 2 to 5 business days and full campaign approval about 1 to 4 weeks, which may affect a 'next week' send date.

SMS benchmarks vary widely by source. Vendor blogs cite 90 to 98% open rates and opt-out rates of 0 to 3.5% per send. Omnisend's 2026 data across 246M+ sends shows a 12.39% average click-through rate and only a 0.12% conversion rate for broadcast SMS campaigns, versus 20.34% and 0.78% for automated flows. Omnisend also notes that standard SMS has no dependable open tracking, and it lists excessive frequency as the top opt-out trigger. No HVAC-specific benchmark was found.

Fall furnace tune-up prices near Frederick run roughly $70 to $200 as a planning range. Maryland-wide guides show about $75 to $200 for a tune-up visit. A Baltimore competitor advertises a $69 'Clean & Check' tune-up and notes that spring and fall are slow seasons when discounts are common. Annual maintenance plans run roughly $150 to $500.

Housecall Pro (the owner's current tool), plan Essentials: $149 per month billed annually, or $189 month to month, for up to 5 users. This price comes from third-party guides citing the vendor's pricing page; the vendor page itself was not retrieved. The same guides list Basic at $59 per month for 1 user and MAX at $299 per month for 8 users. Sources disagree on whether SMS or email Campaigns come with Essentials or only with MAX, and add-on prices are not published. Postcards are reported at about $0.86 to $1.09 each.

Jobber, add-on Marketing Suite (campaigns, reviews, referrals): $99 per month on plans below Plus, per Jobber's own pricing page. Jobber describes it as a customized marketing plan, and third-party sources say it uses AI recommendations that the owner approves before anything goes live. It is included in the Plus plan, and Jobber would replace Housecall Pro rather than sit alongside it.

SimpleTexting (SMS marketing platform), entry plan: reported at $39 per month for 500 credits, with a $4 one-time carrier registration, $10 per month for a number, $20 per month per seat beyond three, and overage around $0.04 to $0.055 per credit. Some sources show $29 per month, so sources conflict. Prices come from third-party roundups, not the vendor page.

Textedly (SMS marketing platform), Basic plan: $29 per month for 500 messages, month to month, with an $8 per month telecom surcharge, so at least about $37 per month. Extra teammates cost $10 per month. Prices come from a third-party review, not the vendor page.

Podium (AI-supported local business messaging platform) does not publish its prices. One 2026 comparison lists Core at $399 per month and Pro at $599 per month, with a custom tier above that, which is well over a $150 per month budget. This is third-party reporting.

open_questions: How many past customers are on the list, and how many have documented written consent to marketing texts? Was consent captured on Housecall Pro forms, invoices, or online booking, and does the wording cover promotional texts?

Does the Housecall Pro campaign or SMS feature, or the AI tool, count as an 'automated system' under the Maryland Act? This is the legal question that decides whether written consent is required, and it needs a lawyer.
What share of the list bought equipment installed by this company, and would a lawyer treat a tune-up offer as covered by the Maryland maintenance-or-repair exemption?

Does the list include numbers on the national or Maryland Do Not Call lists, landlines, disconnected numbers, or customers who previously replied STOP to appointment reminders? The 'revoke all' handling of past opt-outs is unclear.
Which Housecall Pro plan is the company on today, and does it already include SMS or email campaigns, or would those cost extra beyond the $150 per month budget?
Is the company's 10DLC brand and campaign registration already complete? If not, can approval (up to 1 to 4 weeks) be done before the planned send date?
What are the tune-up price and margin, how many open slots does the fall schedule have, and what response rate would fill them? The HVAC-specific SMS conversion rate is unknown.
Do the 4 technicians have capacity if the response is much larger than expected, so that service quality and repair work do not suffer?
Does the company hold any liability or cyber/TCPA insurance coverage that would respond to a text-messaging claim?

industry_expert.headline: Yes to a fall promo, but not a blast to the whole list next week.
industry_expert.summary: A fall tune-up promo is smart, and the schedule needs filling. But blasting every past customer by text next week risks Maryland penalties that scale per text. Send only to customers with written marketing-text consent, reach the rest by postcard, email or calls, and start collecting written opt-ins on every job. Confirm the legal rules with a Maryland attorney first.
key_points: Maryland requires prior express written consent for marketing texts sent through an automated system, and the exemptions are narrow (F1, F3).
Private suits carry $500 or more per violation, up to triple if knowing, so a whole-list blast multiplies exposure (F2, F4).
Postcards cost about $0.86 to $1.09 each (F8), a workable reach for customers without consent. Tune-ups sell for about $70 to $200 (F7), so a few booked jobs cover the cost.
risks: A mass text to non-consented contacts could trigger per-text lawsuits and fines, which could cost far more than the promo earns.
10DLC approval can take 1 to 4 weeks (F5), so a next-week send may not even be allowed to go out.
Too many texts drive opt-outs, and an opt-out revokes all future marketing texts (F4, F6), shrinking the list you rely on for later seasons.
industry_expert.pushback: You assume past customers are reachable and mostly willing to hear from you by text. Check how many actually gave written marketing consent before assuming the list is usable at all.}

ai_tools_expert.headline: Don't blast the whole list; text only consented customers after legal review.
ai_tools_expert.summary: A blast to every past customer risks large per-text penalties under Maryland and federal law, and nobody has confirmed the list has consent. Start with customers who gave written marketing-text consent, reach others by email, postcard or phone, and start collecting written opt-ins on every job. A tune-up promo is worth doing, but not this way next week.
key_points: Maryland requires prior express written consent for marketing texts sent through an automated system, and private lawsuits can reach $500 per violation, up to triple if willful (F1, F2).
Federal exposure is $500 per text, or $1,500 if willful, so the damage grows with every number on the list (F4).
Texting from a standard number needs 10DLC registration, which can take 1 to 4 weeks and may delay a next-week send (F5).
risks: Texting people without documented written consent could cost far more than the promo would earn (F1, F2, F4).
Broadcast SMS converts poorly, at about 0.12% in general benchmarks, and HVAC-specific data is unknown, so response may be thin (F6).
Sending a large blast could push 4 technicians past capacity and hurt service quality on repair calls.
ai_tools_expert.pushback: Assumes the past-customer list has usable written consent; if it lacks it, the whole text plan fails before any tool matters.

baseline_research:
# Recommendation

**Don't blast the whole list by text next week.** Run a smaller, consent-based campaign instead. Text only customers with documented written marketing-text consent, and reach everyone else by email, phone calls, or a targeted postcard. Have a lawyer review the consent language before you expand texting to more of the list.

This is mostly a legal and timing problem, not an objection to AI tools. The upside of a blast is modest and the downside is large.

## Why

**1. Maryland law is strict, and customers can sue.**
- Marketing texts sent through an "automated system" need prior express written consent (F1).
- Since April 2024, customers can sue for the greater of $500 or actual damages per violation, up to triple for willful violations. The older federal-TCPA route adds $500 per violation plus attorney fees (F2, F4).
- Exposure scales with the number of texts. As an illustration, a 2,000-person list with no valid consent could mean a theoretical $1 million or more in claims, against a few thousand dollars of possible tune-up revenue.
- There may be an exemption for maintenance or repair of goods you previously sold. Whether it covers tune-ups on equipment you installed, and on customers you only repaired, is an open legal question (F3). Don't bet the company on an unconfirmed reading.

**2. The timeline doesn't work anyway.** Texting from a business number requires 10DLC registration. Brand approval takes about 2–5 business days and campaign approval 1–4 weeks (F5). If you aren't already registered, "next week" probably isn't realistic.

**3. The expected payoff from a blast is modest.**
- Vendor claims of 90%+ open rates are marketing talk. Omnisend's large dataset shows broadcast SMS converting at about 0.12% (F6).
- There is no HVAC-specific benchmark, so treat this as a rough guide. A blast to 2,000 people might book only a handful of jobs, and I'd plan for single digits to low dozens.
- Tune-ups sell for roughly $70–$200, and competitors discount in the fall (F7). Each job is small, though a tune-up can lead to repair or replacement work.

**4. Your budget limits the tool choices.**
- Housecall Pro Essentials alone is about $149/month (F8). Check what you already pay and whether campaigns are included.
- Jobber would replace Housecall Pro rather than add to it (F9). Podium is far over budget (F12).
- Standalone SMS tools like SimpleTexting and Textedly run roughly $30–$45/month before overages (F10, F11). Prices come from third-party sources, so confirm them.
- Postcards at about $0.86–$1.09 each (F8) are affordable only for a targeted segment, not a whole large list.

## Main risks

- **Legal:** texting people without valid written consent, or texting people who already replied STOP. An opt-out from a marketing text revokes consent for all future marketing texts (F4).
- **Rules inside the send:** Maryland bars solicitations from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. and caps contacts at three in 24 hours on the same subject (F1). Your tool must enforce this, so don't assume it does.
- **Unknowns about your own list:** unknown consent wording, landlines, Do Not Call numbers, and disconnected numbers.
- **Reputation:** excessive frequency is the top opt-out trigger (F6), and unwanted texts can lead to bad reviews.
- **Capacity:** with 4 technicians, a surge of tune-ups could crowd out higher-margin repair and install work. Cap the slots you offer.
- **Insurance:** you may not have coverage for a text-messaging claim. Check your policy.

## Next steps

**This week**
1. Export your customer list from Housecall Pro. Mark who has documented written consent to marketing texts (booking form, signed work order, or online form), and where it came from. Remove anyone who ever replied STOP, plus landlines and bad numbers.
2. Find out which Housecall Pro plan you're on and whether it includes campaigns. Ask support whether you're already 10DLC-registered.
3. Book a short consult with a Maryland attorney. Ask whether the maintenance-or-repair exemption covers your tune-up offer, whether your current consent language covers promotional texts, and whether your tool counts as an "automated system."

**Launch for fall (next 1–2 weeks)**
4. Make the offer a clear, modest one. Consider a tune-up around $79–$129, or a tune-up bundled with a maintenance plan, rather than the lowest price in town. Limit it to the number of slots you actually want to fill.
5. Contact customers who haven't consented by email (nearly free) and by calls from your office staff. Check the Do Not Call lists first. Use postcards only for your best segment, such as customers with equipment 8+ years old or those who bought equipment from you. At about $1 each, 300 postcards costs roughly $300, so budget accordingly.
6. If you're already registered for texting, text the consented segment only. Include your business name, the offer, and opt-out instructions. Send between 9 a.m. and 7 p.m. and don't repeat the message more than once or twice.

**Ongoing**
7. Start collecting written text opt-ins on every job, on the work order, in the Housecall Pro booking flow, and at payment, using wording the lawyer approves.
8. If you want a standalone SMS tool, choose one with built-in opt-in/opt-out handling and 10DLC support in the $30–$50/month range. Do a staged send, starting with consented contacts and expanding as consent grows.
9. Track results: slots filled, cost per booked job, opt-out rate, and any complaints. Use those numbers to decide whether to scale up.

## What would change my view

If most of your list gave clear written consent to marketing texts, and your lawyer confirms the wording, you could text them sooner, once 10DLC registration is done. If the lawyer confirms the maintenance exemption covers your customers, a broader send becomes more defensible. Even then I'd stage it rather than blast everyone at once.

*I'm not a lawyer. Treat the legal points as reasons to get a short professional review, not as legal advice.*
